title: Grading ≠ Feedback, and Sometimes You Don’t Need to Do Either
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that teachers cannot raise the volume and quality of student writing until they separate grading from feedback and decide which one a given assignment actually needs. Using a tennis analogy, he claims that feedback, not scoring, is what improves writers, and that grades only help when students understand what a grade means. He treats grading as something to satisfice, aiming to be fair, consistent, dispassionate, and fast, while keeping his real attention on the Foundations Framework. The key move is to sort assignments by purpose: only work aimed at improving writing quality needs feedback, and work aimed at increasing writing volume often needs neither feedback nor a grade. His daily quickwrite warm-ups illustrate this, since he circulates, teaches toward what he sees, and rarely grades, yet the class adds thousands of words of writing over a semester. The piece is a practical argument for protecting teacher time so that writing-heavy routines are sustainable.
points: Teachers resist increasing writing volume because it conjures stacks of papers to grade, so decoupling grading from writing practice is what makes volume sustainable.
Feedback is what makes writers better, and a score only functions as feedback when students understand what it means.
Only assignments whose goal is improving writing quality need feedback; assignments meant to increase quantity often need neither feedback nor a grade.
Stuart satisfices grading, aiming to be fair, consistent, dispassionate, and fast, because individual class grades matter less than the literacy work itself.
Provisional daily quickwrites, monitored by walking the room and teaching toward observed weaknesses, add thousands of words per semester with almost no grading.
quotes: Until we get smarter about grading, feedback, and when to use which, we won’t meaningfully increase the quantity and quality of writing our students are expected to do. Teachers are already stressed, already pressed for time, and if every time they hear “increase writing volume” they see stacks of to-be-graded papers in their minds, then they are not going to be able to sustain writing-oriented efforts.

Scoring in a tennis match, of course, can be feedback, and insomuch as it is it will help the player get better. Grades can also be feedback when our students have a strong understanding of what their grade on a particular assignment means.

At the GPA level, grades are significant; at the individual class level, grades are less so. Grading is something that I satisfice; my goal is to be fair, consistent, dispassionate, and fast when it comes to grading.

To illustrate that last point, consider the daily quickwrite warm-ups that I use: classic examples of provisional writing at the bottom of the Pyramid of Priorities. I can use these warm-ups to activate prior knowledge, review previously learned material, evaluate cause/effect relationships, or whatever else I think will reinforce the knowledge and the skills I want my students to master.

I walk around the room occasionally during the warm-up time (after I’ve taken attendance) to see what they’re doing, how organized they’re keeping their warm-ups, whether they’re getting bad habits — and then I quickly teach toward what I want to see them do better. This walking around makes it so that I rarely even give a grade for this assignment, which over the course of a semester adds several thousand words to the amount of writing they do in my class.
